title: NAPCC, Missions and India’s NDCs

cards.h: India’s own plan is the core of GS-III climate
cards.b:
Questions ask for the eight NAPCC missions, the targets of the NDC, the five-point Panchamrit and net-zero 2070. The newest NDC was filed in 2026, so recent facts matter.

Always say which NDC you mean: 2015, 2022 or the 2031–35 update.

The National Action Plan on Climate Change has eight missions: Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.

States prepare State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCC). Critics say the missions got uneven funding and weak monitoring.

• Cut emission intensity of GDP by 33 to 35 percent by 2030 from 2005.
  • 40 percent of installed electric capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030.
  • Create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2e through forests.

At COP26 (2021), India announced: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50 percent of energy needs from renewables by 2030; cut projected emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030; cut emission intensity by 45 percent; and net-zero by 2070.

The updated NDC (August 2022) raised the targets: 45 percent intensity cut and 50 percent non-fossil electric capacity by 2030. India reached 50 percent non-fossil installed capacity in mid-2025, about five years early.

The Cabinet approved India’s new NDC in March 2026 and it was submitted to the UNFCCC in April 2026 (as of 2026; reported figures). Reports state two headline goals: at least 47 percent cut in the emission intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2035 and about 60 percent non-fossil electric capacity by 2035.

India filed after most G20 members and long after the September 2025 expected date. The target is an intensity goal, not an absolute cap on emissions.

India’s Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy was submitted at COP27 (2022). The International Solar Alliance (2015, HQ Gurugram) and CDRI (2019) are Indian-led. Mission LiFE (2022) promotes sustainable lifestyles.

India’s climate finance need is estimated in trillions of dollars, and it argues most must come from developed countries.

India’s emission intensity fell by about 33 percent between 2005 and 2019, according to its reporting to the UNFCCC, and non-fossil capacity targets have been met early. The forest carbon sink target is harder: the 2.5 to 3 billion tonne goal depends on forest quality and plantation survival.

Absolute emissions are still rising with the economy, which is why the intensity form of the target draws comment.

Supporters point to rapid solar growth, early targets met and low per capita emissions. Critics note that coal still dominates power, intensity targets allow absolute emissions to rise, and the 2070 net-zero date is later than many.

India says it is doing its fair share and that finance, not ambition, is the gap.

The MoEFCC is the nodal ministry. The Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change oversees. Missions are run by ministries: MNRE (solar), BEE (energy efficiency), Ministry of Jal Shakti (water).

Bureau of Energy Efficiency runs the PAT scheme, now being replaced by carbon trading.

Mains-style: “Critically examine India’s updated NDC. Is it consistent with equity and ambition?” Structure: targets (give years); progress (50 percent non-fossil capacity); gaps (coal, finance, intensity not cap); equity argument; way forward.

Mains-style: “What are the missions under the NAPCC? How successful have they been?”

Prelims tip: NAPCC 2008, eight missions. Panchamrit at COP26. LTS at COP27. ISA HQ Gurugram.
